overview.title: Important Agriculture And Income Support Schemes
overview.definition: Comprehensive overview of direct benefit transfers, price support mechanisms, and financial cushioning policies designed by the state to mitigate agrarian distress, ensure minimum guaranteed returns, and alleviate rural poverty in India.
overview.importanceInUpsc: Directly relevant for GS Paper III (Indian Economy, Agriculture, Subsidies, Minimum Support Prices, and Food Security) as well as Prelims factual questions regarding scheme eligibility, funding patterns, and nodal ministries.
learningOutcomes: Master foundational concepts and mechanisms of Important Agriculture And Income Support Schemes.
Evaluate spatial distribution, institutional frameworks, and policy dimensions.
Apply high-yield mnemonics to solve tricky Prelims and Mains questions.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of Indian agriculture sector

sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Income Support vs Price Support**: **Price Support** (like MSP) operates via market intervention and procurement to protect farmers from price crashes, whereas **Income Support** (like PM-KISAN) provides direct cash transfers to augment farmers' financial needs irrespective of market fluctuations.
• **Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) vs Central Sector Schemes (CS)**: Income support schemes are predominantly **Central Sector Schemes** (100% funding by the Union Government), ensuring seamless nationwide execution without state-level fiscal friction.
• **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)**: Utilization of Aadhaar seeding, Jan Dhan accounts, and mobile platforms to eliminate intermediaries, plug leakages, and ensure direct transfer of funds to beneficiaries.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Share of institutional credit and direct income transfers in total farm household income to gauge vulnerability against agrarian distress and monsoon shocks.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: 100% Central Sector Scheme; provides Rs. 6,000 per year in three equal 4-monthly installments to all landholding farmer families.
Data verified through land records; direct transfer via Aadhaar-linked Public Financial Management System (PFMS).
Frequently targeted in Prelims regarding exclusions (institutional landholders, income taxpayers, constitutional post holders).
PM-KUSUM (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan)
Promotes solar pumps, grid-connected solar power plants on barren lands, and solarization of grid-connected agriculture pumps.
Subsidies shared between Centre (30%), States (30%), and Bank loans/Farmer contribution (40%).
Crucial for Mains linkages between renewable energy transition, groundwater conservation, and discom debt reduction.
Comprehensive crop insurance scheme replacing NAIS/MNAIS with uniform low premium (2% Kharif, 1.5% Rabi, 5% Commercial/Horticulture).
Actuarial premium shared between Centre and States on 50:50 basis (North-Eastern states 90:10).
High-yield Prelims questions on premium rates, voluntary vs compulsory status, and technology utilization (remote sensing, smartphones).

items.definition: Certain categories are excluded: institutional landholders, former/present ministers, MPs, MLAs, mayors, serving/retired central/state government employees (except multi-tasking staff), income tax payers of the last assessment year, and professionals like doctors, engineers, and lawyers.

Provides short-term crop loans up to Rs. 3 lakh to farmers at a subsidized interest rate of 7% per annum, with an additional 3% prompt repayment incentive, bringing the effective interest rate down to 4%.
A medium-long term debt financing facility for investment in viable projects for post-harvest management infrastructure and community farming assets with interest subvention and credit guarantee.

items.term: PM-AASHA (Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan)
items.definition: Umbrella scheme comprising Price Support Scheme (PSS), Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS), and Private Procurement & Stockist Scheme (PPSS) to ensure remunerative prices for agricultural produce.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Rainfed and Arid Zones**: Focus areas for PM-KUSUM solar pump installations (e.g., Rajasthan, Western UP) to mitigate erratic grid supply and diesel dependency.
• **High Procurement States**: Punjab, Haryana, and Madhya Pradesh dominate procurement-based income/price support mechanisms, whereas Eastern India (Bihar, West Bengal) heavily benefits from direct cash transfers like PM-KISAN due to fragmented landholdings.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Incomplete land record digitisation, exclusion errors, delayed premium settlements in crop insurance, and fiscal stress on state exchequers.
• **Policy Integration**: Convergence of PM-KISAN with digital public infrastructure (AgriStack, Krishi Decision Support System) for precision agriculture and targeted benefit delivery.

items.title: Mnemonic for PMFBY Premium Rates
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'Koris Rabbi Commercialized 5 Stars' -> **Ko** (Kharif = 2%), **R** (Rabi = 1.5%), **Commercial** (Commercial/Horticulture = 5%).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Instantly recalls the exact percentage shares paid by farmers as premium under PMFBY.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Eliminates confusion in numerical matching questions frequently asked by UPSC.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Income support = 100% Central Sector (PM-KISAN); Insurance/Infrastructure = Centrally Sponsored (Cost sharing between Centre and States).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often traps aspirants by stating that PM-KISAN is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme requiring state matching grants. Remember, it is a 100% Central Sector Scheme funded entirely by the Government of India.

Mains Value Addition: In GS-III answers on farm distress, advocate for a shift from input subsidies (power, fertilizer) to direct income support (PM-KISAN) coupled with capital investment in infrastructure (AIF) to ensure fiscal prudence and ecological sustainability.

keyTakeaways: Direct income support schemes like PM-KISAN provide critical liquidity cushion to small and marginal farmers but cannot replace long-term structural reforms.
Financing mechanisms under schemes like PM-KUSUM and AIF bridge the gap between energy security, post-harvest losses, and farm income augmentation.
Precision in identifying beneficiary exclusions and integrating digital land records are vital for plug-and-play execution of agricultural welfare policies.
